At a hearing held today, Apple is challenging the UK government's decision to refuse to publicly confirm whether it has ever issued a request to access users' encrypted data. Details are as follows.

Some background information

Earlier last year, The Washington Post reported that the UK government had secretly ordered Apple to build a backdoor into all content uploaded by global users to iCloud.

The order itself is subject to strict confidentiality rules, and Apple is further prohibited from publicly confirming or discussing the request.

The UK government has long maintained a policy of 'neither confirm nor deny' regarding the existence of individual orders, and companies that receive such orders are likewise prohibited from disclosing that they have received one.

According to reports, after receiving but not confirming the order, Apple removed the option for UK iCloud users to enable Advanced Data Protection (ADP).

The reason is that once ADP is enabled, iCloud backups and other categories of iCloud data are protected by end-to-end encryption. Therefore, Apple chose not to offer ADP to new UK users rather than comply with the UK's backdoor order—even though the order reportedly applies to global users.

At this stage, the standoff between Apple and the UK government has split into two fronts: one is challenging the fundamental request to access encrypted data, and the other is opposing the 'gagging order' that prohibits it from being publicly discussed.

In April 2025, a judge rejected the UK government's attempt to keep the basic details of Apple's legal challenge secret, ruling that disclosure of the very existence of the case would not harm national security.

Months later, under pressure from the White House, the UK government withdrew its request to access American users' data under its secret powers. However, the request did not disappear entirely: the UK subsequently issued a new notice specifically targeting Apple users located within the UK.

Several weeks later, there were reports that after the original global order was replaced by the new order targeting UK users, Apple had launched a second round of legal action against the UK government.

Speaking of which, that brings us to today's latest developments.

Apple challenges the confidentiality arrangements of the order

According to Reuters, Apple challenged the UK government's continued refusal to confirm or deny the existence of a new 'Technical Capability Notice' at the Investigatory Powers Tribunal (IPT) in London today.

According to Reuters, Apple's representative lawyers argued that the government's confidentiality policy hinders meaningful public discussion of the case and undermines the principle of open justice.

The following is an excerpt from the report:

At the hearing held at the Investigatory Powers Tribunal on Thursday, Ben Jaffey, a lawyer representing the advocacy groups Privacy International and Liberty, described the government's position as having become 'absurd.' He pointed out that 'the truth is already out,' meaning the relevant information is openly available in the public domain. He noted that American politicians and officials have publicly mentioned the original notice, while anonymous UK government sources have also confirmed the matter to the media. Both he and Apple's lawyers believe that the UK government's 'neither confirm nor deny' policy is an insult to open justice and hinders meaningful public discussion on the matter.

It is worth noting that the focus of today's hearing was on the confidentiality arrangements of the order, rather than the fundamental legal question of whether the UK government had the original authority to request access to Apple's encrypted data.

After today's hearing concludes, the Investigatory Powers Tribunal will issue a ruling on whether the government can continue to maintain its 'neither confirm nor deny' policy in this case. According to Reuters, the formal hearing on Apple's challenge to the Technical Capability Notice itself is not expected to take place until sometime next year.
